title: Logit-Weight Scores, Features vs Neurons
takeaway: Given only a written explanation of a unit, Claude predicts which unseen tokens that unit promotes with 0.74 mean accuracy for autoencoder features and 0.58 for MLP neurons, against a 0.5 chance baseline. The neuron distribution piles up on the chance line while the feature distribution spreads toward 1.0. The "failures" counts in the legend are parsing failures of the scoring harness, not low scores.
walkthrough:
The chart is two overlapping histograms of one accuracy score, computed over two populations of units drawn from the same model.

One population is the surviving directions learned by the [[sparse-autoencoder]] on the MLP activations of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]]. The other is that model's 512 MLP neurons. The comparison is the paper's standing one: its unit of analysis against the default unit.

### The task being scored

This is the logit half of [[automated-interpretability]], called [[automated-logit-scoring]]. Every [[feature]] and neuron already carries a written explanation that Claude produced earlier from examples of where it fires. That explanation is reused here, unchanged, for a different question.

Each unit has a [[logit-weight]] vector — one number per vocabulary token, saying how much the unit's firing pushes that next-token logit up or down. The scorer sees 100 tokens per unit. Fifty come from the 10th through 60th largest positive logit weights, with the top ten withheld because they were shown when the explanation was written. Fifty are random tokens.

Claude labels each token yes or no: from the explanation alone, would this token plausibly come next? Accuracy is the fraction of the 100 labels that are right. Because the mix is 50/50, blind guessing lands at 0.5 — the dotted "random chance" line.

### Reading the axes

The horizontal axis is that accuracy. The vertical axis is density: each histogram integrates to 1 over its own population, so height is share per unit of accuracy, not a count. Bars are about 0.02 wide, so a bar of height 4.0 holds roughly $4.0 \times 0.02 = 0.08$, eight percent of that population.

Crimson is features, teal is neurons, and the dark navy band is where the two translucent layers sit on top of each other. The small triangles below the axis mark the two medians.

### What it shows

The neuron histogram has a tall spike planted on the chance line. Many neurons score near 0.5, meaning the explanation buys nothing about what they promote; [[polysemanticity]] is the paper's account of why a neuron resists a single explanation. Their median is 0.53 and their mean 0.58, the mean pulled up by a thinner right tail.

The feature histogram puts its weight to the right, with a broad band of mass between 0.8 and 1.0. Median 0.73, mean 0.74.

### The failure counts

"Failures" are not low scores. They count runs where Claude did not reply in the format the scoring code could read, so the unit was dropped rather than scored. The rates are about 4% of features and 6% of neurons, and they say something about the harness, not about the units. As a floor comparison, the appendix reports the [[randomized-transformer]] features scoring at 0.5 on this same task.

terms.definition: The chart's title. It names the experiment: scoring feature and neuron explanations by whether they predict the tokens the unit pushes up, rather than by whether they predict where the unit fires.
The horizontal axis. For one feature or neuron, it is the fraction of 100 yes/no token judgements that Claude got right, so it runs from 0.0 to 1.0 and moves in steps of 0.01.

The vertical axis. Each histogram is normalised so its bars integrate to 1 over its own population, letting 3,676-odd features and 512 neurons be compared on the same panel despite very different counts.
The label on the dotted vertical line at 0.5. Because the 100 candidate tokens are a deliberate 50/50 mix of high-logit and random tokens, a scorer answering blindly averages 0.5.
The crimson population and its legend box: the directions learned by the A/1 sparse autoencoder on the one-layer model's MLP activations, excluding the dead and ultralow-density ones.
The teal population and its legend box: the 512 ReLU neurons of the same one-layer transformer's MLP, scored by the identical procedure as the control.
The middle accuracy of each population, marked by the small triangle under the axis. It is the statistic least disturbed by the spike sitting on the chance line.
The average accuracy across a population. It is the number quoted in the body text as "74% average across features, compared to a 58% average across neurons".

The count of units whose scoring run was discarded because Claude did not reply in the format the scoring code could parse. It is a formatting and parsing outcome, not an accuracy value, and those units contribute no bar to the histogram.
The legend entry for the two small triangles below the horizontal axis, one per population, placed at that population's median accuracy.
Not a third population. It is the colour produced where the translucent crimson and teal histograms cover the same accuracy bin, so it marks the range where features and neurons both have mass.
Anthropic's language model, used here in two roles: it wrote the feature explanations, and it is the scorer answering yes/no on each candidate token.

For one feature or neuron, a vector with one entry per vocabulary token giving how much that unit's firing raises or lowers the next-token logit, computed along the direct path from the MLP output through the unembedding.
A candidate token drawn from that logit-weight vector. The positive half of the sample comes from the 10th to 60th largest positive weights; the other half is drawn at random from the rest.

The short natural-language description of a unit that Claude wrote earlier from examples of where the unit activates. It is the only information the scorer gets about the unit here, which is what makes this a cross-check of the activation-based explanation.
The paper's name for its main dictionary-learning run: the 4,096-feature sparse autoencoder trained on the one-layer transformer's MLP activations. It supplies the crimson population.

numbers.meaning: Median accuracy across features. Half the scored features do better than this on judging whether an unseen token is one they promote.

Mean accuracy across features, quoted in the body text as 74%. The appendix separately reports the feature median as 0.74 rather than the 0.73 printed here; the paper does not reconcile the one-point gap.
Median accuracy across neurons, barely above the 0.5 chance line — the median neuron's explanation predicts its promoted tokens about as well as guessing.
Mean accuracy across neurons, quoted in the body text as 58%. It sits above the neuron median because a right tail of easier neurons pulls the average up while the bulk stays at chance.
Feature failures: 152 of the 3,676 features the task was attempted on produced a reply Claude did not format correctly for scoring, about 4.1%. They were dropped, not scored zero.

The number of features entering the logit task. It is close to the 4,096 learned features minus the 168 dead and 292 ultralow-density ones the paper excludes from global analysis (3,636); the paper does not explain the small difference.
Neuron failures: 31 of the 512 MLP neurons, about 6.1%, hit the same formatting problem. That the neuron rate is higher than the feature rate carries no claim about neurons — it is scorer behaviour.
The neuron population, which is the full MLP width of the one-layer transformer under study. Every neuron is evaluated, so this is a census rather than a sample.
The number of features in the A/1 autoencoder, from which 168 dead and 292 ultralow-density features are excluded before global analysis.

The chance line. It sits at 0.5 because the 100 candidate tokens are half high-logit and half random, so a coin flip is right half the time. The appendix also reports the randomized-transformer features scoring at 0.5 here, as expected from shuffled weights.
Candidate tokens judged per unit: 50 taken from the 10th to 60th largest positive logit weights and 50 drawn at random. This fixes both the chance rate and the 0.01 granularity of the accuracy score.
The number of top logit tokens held out. They were shown to Claude when the explanation was written, so scoring on them would test recall rather than prediction.
The range of the accuracy axis, tick-marked every 0.1. Values below 0.5 mean the explanation did worse than guessing on that unit.
The range of the density axis. The tallest bar, the teal neuron spike straddling 0.5, reaches roughly 4.0; with bars about 0.02 wide that bar holds around 8% of all scored neurons.
The accuracy band where the crimson feature histogram keeps a broad shelf of mass, with local heights around 1.0 to 1.5 density. Neurons have very little mass there.
